description:
Used to politely ask for something in a shop, café, or restaurant. Put the item in front of 주세요.

Rule: 주세요 asks for an object. To ask someone to do something instead, attach -아/어 주세요 to a verb — 도와주세요 (please help me).

examples.en: Water, please.
Please give me the menu.
Please give me the receipt.

description:
Used to ask what something is when you don't know its name. Point at it and add 뭐예요?

Rule: 뭐 ends in a vowel, so it always takes 예요, never 이에요.

examples.en: What is this?
What is that?
What is this food?

description:
Used to ask whether something exists or is available. It covers both 'is there' and 'do you have'.

Rule: Use 있어요? for things and places. When asking whether a person is in, 계세요? is the respectful form.

examples.en: Is there Wi-Fi?
Is there a seat?
Is there a restroom?

description:
Used to ask the way to a place. Put the destination in front, with no particle needed.

Rule: This asks for the route. To ask which transport to take, use 뭐 타고 가요?

examples.en: How do I get to Hongdae?
How do I get to Myeongdong?
How do I get to the airport?

description:
Used to name a place you'd like to visit. The particle 에 is usually dropped in speech.

Rule: -고 싶어요 works only for your own wish. To talk about what someone else wants, use -고 싶어 해요.

examples.en: I want to go to Jeju Island.
I want to go to Hongdae!
I want to go to the Han River.

description:
Used to ask someone's opinion, or how something is going. Put the topic in front.

Rule: It doubles as a suggestion — 커피 어때요? can mean 'How about coffee?' depending on the situation.

examples.en: How is this food?
How is this café?
How is life in Korea?

description:
Used to settle on one option when ordering or choosing between things.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 으로 할게요 (김밥으로 할게요). After a vowel or ㄹ, use 로 할게요 (커피로 할게요).

examples.en: I'll go with an Americano.
I'll go with this one.
I'll go with the large size.

description:
Used to ask whether someone has ever had a particular experience.

Rule: Attach -아/어 본 적 있어요? to a verb stem. Answer with 있어요 (I have) or 없어요 (I haven't) rather than 네 or 아니요.

examples.en: Have you ever tried samgyeopsal?
Have you ever been to a noraebang?
Have you ever worn a hanbok?

description:
Used to ask someone for a recommendation. Put the category in front — a food, a place, a show.

Rule: Keep 주세요 on the end. Without it, 추천해요 becomes a statement meaning 'I recommend it'.

examples.en: Please recommend samgyeopsal!
Please recommend a café.
Please recommend a Korean drama.

description:
Used to make a polite request, noticeably softer than -아/어 주세요.

Rule: Attach -아/어 주실 수 있어요? to a verb stem. 주실 carries an honorific, so it suits strangers and people senior to you.

examples.en: Could you take a photo for me?
Could you help me?
Could you explain a bit more?
examples.ko: 조금 더 설명해 주실 수 있어요?

description:
Used to say what you like or enjoy. Put the thing in front.

Rule: 좋아해요 is a verb and takes 을/를 (한국 음식을 좋아해요). 좋아요 is an adjective and takes 이/가 (한국 음식이 좋아요).

examples.en: I like K-pop!
I like Korean food.
I really like this song.

description:
Used when something strikes you as new and wonderful — a common reaction when you first meet a different culture.

Rule: 신기해요 is about novelty and wonder. If you mean something is odd or off, use 이상해요 (that's strange) instead.

examples.en: Korean culture is really fascinating!
I've never seen this food before — it's fascinating.
It's fascinating how thorough the recycling is.

description:
Used to ask for a refill or a second helping. In Korean restaurants, side dishes usually come free this way.

Rule: 더 goes right before 주세요, not before the noun — 김치 더 주세요, not 더 김치 주세요.

examples.en: Please give me more kimchi!
Please give me more water.
Please give me more side dishes.

description:
Used to ask for a discount when haggling.

Rule: This belongs at traditional markets and street stalls. Prices are fixed at department stores and chain shops, so it isn't used there.

examples.en: Please give me a small discount!
Please knock off just 1,000 won.
Please give me a discount if I buy two.

description:
Used to ask whether someone has tried out a product.

Rule: 써 보다 is for things you use — cosmetics, apps, tools. For food say 먹어 봤어요?, and for clothes 입어 봤어요?

examples.en: Have you tried this serum?
Have you tried this app?
Have you tried Korean cosmetics?

description:
Used to ask which option the other person prefers.

Rule: 어떤 asks 'which one' among options you can see. 무슨 asks 'what kind' in general.

examples.en: Which color do you like?
Which style do you like?
Which one is tastier?

description:
Used when something turns out different from what you had in mind.

Rule: 생각보다 goes at the front and the adjective follows. Whether it means more or less depends on that adjective — 생각보다 맵지 않아요 means less spicy.

examples.en: It's tastier than I expected!
It's not as hard as I thought.
It's faster than I expected!

description:
Used to express warmth about everyone being gathered in one place.

Rule: -아/어서 좋아요 attaches any reason to 좋아요 (it's good) — 날씨가 좋아서 좋아요 means 'I'm happy because the weather is nice'.

examples.en: I'm so happy we're all together!
I'm happy to be together with my whole family.
It's great to be together with all my friends!

description:
Used to say something has already happened, often to stop someone from doing it again.

Rule: 이미 normally comes with a past-tense verb — 이미 먹었어요 (I already ate). 벌써 also means 'already', but adds surprise at how soon it happened.

examples.en: I already ate.
I already knew!
I already made a reservation.

description:
Used for the flutter you feel before something important. It covers both nerves and excitement.

Rule: 떨려요 describes your own feeling and takes no object. To give the cause, put it in front with -아/어서 or -라서 (첫 발표라서 떨려요).

examples.en: I'm nervous because it's my first presentation.
I'm so nervous — will it be okay?
My heart is pounding — I'm so nervous!

description:
Used to say which country or city you come from.

Rule: 에서 marks a starting point, so it attaches to the place (미국에서 왔어요). Do not use 에, which marks a destination.

examples.en: I'm from the United States.
I'm from Seoul.
I'm from Busan.

description:
A set greeting used when you meet someone you'll be working or studying with. English has no direct equivalent — it asks for their goodwill.

Rule: 부탁드려요 is the humble form of 부탁해요. In formal settings such as an interview or presentation, use 잘 부탁드립니다.

examples.en: Please take care of me!
I look forward to working with you.
Please take care of me today!

description:
Used to ask where to board a bus, subway line, or shuttle.

Rule: 어디서 marks the place where an action happens. If you only want to know where something is, use 어디예요?

examples.en: Where do I get on Line 2?
Where do I get on the bus?
Where do I get on the airport bus?

description:
Used to say what you feel like eating.

Rule: -고 싶어요 attaches to a verb stem and speaks only for yourself. For another person's craving, use -고 싶어 해요.

examples.en: I want to eat samgyeopsal!
I want to eat tteokbokki.
I want to eat naengmyeon!

description:
Used to say you cannot eat something, whether because of an allergy, a religion, or your tolerance for spice.

Rule: 못 goes right before the verb and means you are unable to. 안 먹어요 means you choose not to.

examples.en: I can't eat shellfish.
I can't eat spicy food.
I can't eat pork.

description:
Used to ask permission before eating or drinking.

Rule: Attach -아/어도 돼요? to a verb stem. The answer comes back as 네, 돼요 (yes, you may) or 아니요, 안 돼요 (no, you may not).

examples.en: Is it okay to eat here?
Is it okay to eat this?
Is it okay to eat now?

english: May I sing ~? / May I call you ~?
description:
Used to ask permission. 부르다 covers both singing a song and calling someone by a name, so the meaning comes from what goes in front.

Rule: For a song, put it straight in front — 이 노래 불러도 돼요? (May I sing this song?). For a name or title, add 라고 after a vowel and 이라고 after a consonant — 언니라고 불러도 돼요? (Can I call you 언니, older sister?).

examples.en: May I sing this song?
May I sing first?
Can I call you 언니 (older sister)?

english: I want to come here again.
description:
Used to tell someone you enjoyed a place enough to return — a natural compliment to a host or a shop.

Rule: 또 means 'again' and goes before the verb. 다시 is close, but 또 sounds warmer in this phrase.

examples.en: I want to come here again!
I want to come back to Korea.
I want to come back to this café!

description:
Used to say which transport you're taking, or to tell someone which one to take.

Rule: Korean says 버스를 타요, not 버스에 타요 — 타다 takes 을/를 even though English says 'get on'. In speech the particle is usually dropped (버스 타요). To get off, use 내려요.

examples.en: Take Line 2!
Take the bus.
Take a taxi.

description:
Used to say which stop or station you're getting off at.

Rule: 에서 marks the place where you get off. Pair it with 타요 for getting on — 2호선 타요, 홍대입구역에서 내려요 means 'take Line 2 and get off at Hongik Univ. Station'.

examples.en: Get off at Hongik University Station.
Get off at the next stop.
Get off here!

description:
Used to tell a taxi driver where you want to go.

Rule: 까지 marks the end point of the trip. 에 가 주세요 also works, but 까지 sounds more natural to a driver.

examples.en: Please take me to Hongdae.
Please take me to the airport.
Please take me to Myeongdong.

description:
Used to ask a restaurant to adjust how your food is prepared.

Rule: Put an adjective stem between 덜 and 게 해 주세요 — 덜 맵게 해 주세요 (please make it less spicy). To ask for more of something instead, swap 덜 (less) for 더 (more).

examples.en: Please make it less spicy.
Please make it less sweet.
Please make it less salty.

english: Can I get a refill of ~?
description:
Used to ask whether something can be refilled. Side dishes, rice, and soup are often free this way in Korea.

Rule: 되다 here means 'is possible'. The answer comes back as 네, 돼요 (yes, you can) or 안 돼요 (no, you can't).

examples.en: Can I get a refill of kimchi?
Can I get a refill of side dishes?
Can I get a refill of water?

description:
Used to ask about someone's plans at a certain time.

Rule: 에 attaches to time words like 주말에 and 저녁에, but never to 오늘, 내일, or 어제 — say 내일 뭐 해요?

examples.en: What are you doing this weekend?
What are you doing tonight?
What are you doing next week?

description:
Used to invite someone to do something with you. It sounds friendly rather than formal.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을래요 (먹을래요?). After a vowel or ㄹ, use -ㄹ래요 (볼래요?).

examples.en: Do you want to eat together?
Do you want to watch a movie together?
Do you want to take a walk together?

english: I think I'll be a little late.
description:
Used to let someone know in advance that you won't arrive on time.

Rule: -을 것 같아요 turns a flat statement into a guess. 늦어요 states plainly 'I'm late', while 늦을 것 같아요 sounds softer and more considerate.

examples.en: I think I'll be a little late.
I think I'll be 10 minutes late.
I think I'll be quite late — sorry.

description:
Used to tell someone you don't know where you are and need help.

Rule: Korean puts this in the past tense (잃었어요) even though English uses the present. 길을 잃어요 sounds wrong.

examples.en: I'm lost, please help me.
I'm lost — where is Hongdae?
I'm lost — can I look at your map?
examples.ko: 길을 잃었어요, 지도 좀 봐도 돼요?

description:
Used when giving directions to say the way is simple — no turns needed.

Rule: -으면 돼요 means 'it's enough to ~'. It makes instructions sound easy and reassuring.

examples.en: Just go straight.
Just go straight down this road.
If you go straight, there's a café.

description:
Used to tell someone which way to turn when giving directions.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 으로 — 오른쪽으로 (to the right). After a vowel or ㄹ, use 로. 돌면 돼요 means the same as 꺾으면 돼요 and is just as common.

examples.en: Turn right over there.
Turn left at the traffic light.
Turn right at the convenience store.

description:
Used to ask whether someone has experienced something before.

Rule: Attach -아/어 봤어요? to a verb stem — 먹어 봤어요?, 가 봤어요?, 입어 봤어요? Without 보다, 봤어요? simply means 'did you see it?'

examples.en: Have you tried sundae?
Have you been to Jeju Island?
Have you watched a Korean drama?

description:
Used for anything enjoyable — a drama, a class, a person, a trip.

Rule: 재미있어요 covers both 'fun' and 'interesting'. To say the opposite, use 재미없어요 (it's boring), written as one word.

examples.en: This drama is really fun!
Studying Korean is interesting.
It's hard but fun!

description:
Slang shortened from 강력 추천, meaning a strong recommendation. You'll see it constantly in reviews and casual chat.

Rule: This is casual. With someone senior, or in writing, use 추천해요 or 추천드려요.

examples.en: I highly recommend this café!
I highly recommend this drama!
I highly recommend this food!

description:
Used to ask about the weather at a place or on a certain day.

Rule: Put the place or time straight in front, with no particle — 서울 날씨 어때요?, 내일 날씨 어때요?

examples.en: What's the weather like today?
What's the weather like in Seoul?
What's the weather like tomorrow?

description:
Used to guess that rain or snow is on the way, based on what you can see.

Rule: In Korean, rain and snow 'come' rather than 'fall' — use 오다 (to come), not 내리다 (to fall). So it's 비 와요 (it's raining), not 비 내려요.

examples.en: It looks like it's going to snow.
It looks like it's going to rain.
It looks like a shower is coming soon.

description:
Used at a pharmacy to ask for medicine for a specific symptom.

Rule: Korean builds medicine names as one word — 두통 (headache) + 약 becomes 두통약, and 감기 (cold) + 약 becomes 감기약. A pharmacy is 약국.

examples.en: Do you have headache medicine?
Do you have digestive medicine?
Do you have cold medicine?

description:
Used to advise someone against eating something, gently rather than as an order.

Rule: -는 게 나아요 means 'it's better to ~'. Put 안 in front of the verb for the negative — 안 먹는 게 나아요. For the positive, drop it — 먹는 게 나아요.

examples.en: It's better not to eat spicy food.
examples.ko: 매운 거 안 먹는 게 나아요.

examples.en: It's better not to eat late.
It's better not to eat greasy food.
examples.ko: 기름진 거 안 먹는 게 나아요.

description:
Used to ask what someone does for fun. It's one of the standard questions when you're getting to know a Korean person.

Rule: 취미 (hobby) takes 가 here, so it's 취미가 뭐예요? Among close friends the casual form is 취미가 뭐야?

examples.en: What are your hobbies?
What are your hobbies these days?
What are your hobbies? Mine is photography!

description:
A quick way to say you feel the same. It works after almost any statement, positive or negative.

Rule: 저도요 is the polite form; among friends say 나도. If you're agreeing with something the other person doesn't like, 저도요 still works — 저도요, 저도 안 좋아해요.

examples.en: Me too! I love K-pop too!
Me too — it's really delicious!
Me too! Let's go together!

description:
Used to say something didn't meet your expectations, without being blunt about it.

Rule: 별로예요 is much softer than 싫어요 (I hate it), so Koreans use it to turn things down politely. The topic goes straight in front with no particle — 이 드라마 별로예요.

examples.en: I don't really like spicy food.
I don't really like this style.
This drama isn't really my thing.

description:
Used to ask what a place is known for — its signature dish, product, or sight.

Rule: 여기서 means 'here at this place'. 게 is a shortened form of 것이 (the thing that), so 유명한 게 means 'the thing that is famous'.

examples.en: What food is this place famous for?
What is this neighborhood famous for?
What are the famous tourist spots in Korea?

description:
Used to suggest taking a picture with someone.

Rule: Korean uses 찍다 (to shoot) for taking photos, never 만들다 or 가지다. Put the place in front with 에서 — 여기서 같이 사진 찍어요.

examples.en: Let's take a photo together!
Let's take a photo together in front of Gyeongbokgung!
Let's take a photo here together!

english: Did the photo turn out well?
description:
Used to ask whether a picture came out nicely — a natural follow-up after taking one.

Rule: Korean says a photo 나오다 (comes out) rather than 되다. 잘 나왔어요 means it turned out well, and 잘 안 나왔어요 means it didn't.

examples.en: Did the photo turn out well?
Did the selfie turn out well?
The photo turned out great — you look pretty!

description:
Used when you meet someone again after a long gap. It's one of the most common Korean greetings.

Rule: The casual form is 오랜만이야. It's usually followed by 잘 지냈어요? (how have you been?) as a set pair.

examples.en: It's been a while! How have you been?
Sophie! Long time no see!
It's been a while — I missed you!

description:
Used when you meet someone again after a while.

Rule: This is past tense (지냈어요), asking about the time since you last met. To ask how someone is right now, use 잘 지내요?

examples.en: Have you been well?
Have you been well lately?
Have you been well? Were you very busy?

description:
A warm goodbye that leaves the door open for another meeting.

Rule: 보다 means both 'see' and 'meet' in Korean, so 봐요 works as a farewell. The casual form is 다음에 또 봐.

examples.en: Let's meet again soon!
We definitely have to meet again!
See you again — today was really fun!

description:
Used to ask a friend how something went — a trip, an exam, a first day.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 어땠어요? Put the topic straight in front with no particle — 시험 어땠어?

examples.en: How was the Han River?
How was the exam?
How was the first day?

english: It was my first time, but ~
description:
Used to set up a contrast between a first experience and how it actually went.

Rule: -인데 attaches background information that the next clause turns around. The polite form is 처음이었는데요, and for something that is your first time right now, use 처음인데.

examples.en: It was my first time, but it was really delicious!
It was my first time, but it was easier than I thought.
It was my first time, but I want to go again!

description:
Used to soften a guess or an opinion so it doesn't sound like a flat assertion. Koreans use it constantly to stay polite.

Rule: The ending changes with the word type. Verbs take -을 것 같아요 for a guess about the future (갈 것 같아요), adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 것 같아요 (좋은 것 같아요), and for the past use -은 것 같아요 (간 것 같아요).

examples.en: It seems like it'll be delicious!
It seems like it'll be difficult.
It seems like it's famous.

description:
Used to guess about someone else's situation from what you can see or hear.

Rule: Verbs take -나 봐요 (오나 봐요). Adjectives take -은가/-ㄴ가 봐요 — 좋은가 봐요 after a consonant, 바쁜가 봐요 after a vowel. Use it about others, not about your own feelings.

examples.en: It must be delicious — the line is long!
It must be famous.
They must be busy.

english: I have to ~ / You have to ~
description:
Used to say something is necessary or unavoidable.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 해야 해요. Attach -아/어야 하다 to a verb stem — 먹어야 해, 가야 해. Adding 꼭 (definitely) in front makes it stronger.

examples.en: You have to study now!
You have to eat.
You absolutely have to go!

description:
Used to tell a friend not to do something. It sounds caring rather than harsh, depending on tone.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is -지 마세요. Attach -지 말다 to a verb stem — 걱정하지 마, 늦지 마.

examples.en: Don't worry!
Don't be late!
Don't give up!

description:
Used to remind a friend about something they might leave behind or overlook.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 잊지 마세요. It uses -지 말다, the same pattern as 하지 마 (don't do it).

examples.en: Don't forget your phone!
Don't forget our appointment!
Don't forget your umbrella!

description:
Used to ask someone's opinion on a specific topic.

Rule: Put the topic straight in front with no particle. Korean asks 어떻게 생각해요? (how do you think), never 무엇을 생각해요? — the 어떻게 is fixed.

examples.en: What do you think about Korean food?
What do you think about this drama?
What do you think about my plan?

description:
Used to acknowledge that what the other person said makes sense, even if you go on to disagree.

Rule: 맞는 말이에요 agrees with the statement rather than the person. To agree with the person themselves, say 맞아요 or 저도 그렇게 생각해요.

examples.en: That's a good point. I think so too.
That's a good point, but I see it differently.
That's a valid point!

description:
Used to state your own preference without contradicting anyone directly — a gentle way to disagree.

Rule: 좀 (a bit) is what softens it. Dropping it — 저는 달라요 — sounds much more blunt.

examples.en: I'm a bit different — I love spicy food!
examples.ko: 저는 좀 달라요, 매운 거 좋아해요!

examples.en: I'm a bit different — I prefer bands.
examples.ko: 저는 좀 달라요, 밴드가 더 좋아요.

examples.en: My taste is a bit different.

description:
Used to ask whether someone has ever visited a place.

Rule: 에 marks the destination, and -아/어 봤어요 adds the sense of having tried it. The answer is 가 봤어요 (I have) or 안 가 봤어요 (I haven't).

examples.en: Have you been to Jeju Island?
Have you been to Gyeongbokgung?
Have you been to Busan?

description:
Used to recommend a place strongly.

Rule: 꼭 means 'without fail' and carries the emphasis. -아/어 보세요 means 'give it a try', so 가 보세요 is warmer than the plain 가세요.

examples.en: You should definitely visit the Han River!
You should definitely check out Gwangjang Market!
You should definitely go to Jeju Island!

english: What are you watching these days?
description:
Used to ask what shows someone is into lately — one of the easiest ways to start a conversation.

Rule: 보다 covers watching and reading alike, so it works for dramas, films, and webtoons. 요즘 means 'these days' and goes at the front.

examples.en: What are you watching lately?
What dramas are you watching lately?
What are you watching lately? Give me a recommendation!

description:
Used when something has completely pulled you in — a drama, a hobby, a genre of music.

Rule: The thing you're hooked on takes 에 — 케이팝에 완전 빠져들었어요. 완전 (totally) is casual emphasis and can be dropped in formal speech.

examples.en: I'm totally hooked on this drama!
I'm totally hooked on K-pop!
I'm totally absorbed in studying Korean.

english: I can't wait for the next episode.
description:
Used to say you're looking forward to what comes next.

Rule: 화 is the counter for episodes, so 다음 화 means 'the next episode'. 기대되다 describes the feeling arising in you, so it takes 가 rather than 를 — 다음 화가 기대돼요.

examples.en: I can't wait for the next episode!
I can't wait for next week!
I can't wait to see the ending!

description:
Used to ask whether someone recognizes a song.

Rule: The negative of 알아요 is 몰라요, not 안 알아요 — Korean uses a separate word. So the answer is 알아요 or 몰라요.

examples.en: Do you know this song?
Do you know this song? I love it so much!
Do you know this singer's songs?

description:
Used to ask what a line of a song means — a natural question when you're learning through music.

Rule: 무슨 뜻이에요? asks for the meaning of a word or phrase. Put the part you're asking about in front with 가/이 — '그리워'가 무슨 뜻이에요?

examples.en: What does this lyric mean?
What does '그리워' mean?
What does this part of the lyrics mean?

description:
Used for a song, snack, or show you can't stop coming back to.

Rule: 중독성 means 'addictiveness', and it pairs with 있다 — 중독성 있어요. Adding 진짜 (really) or 완전 (totally) in front makes it stronger.

examples.en: This song is so catchy!
Tteokbokki is so addictive!
This drama is totally addictive!

english: How do you take care of ~?
description:
Used to ask about someone's routine for looking after something — skin, hair, health.

Rule: 관리 means 'care' or 'upkeep' and takes 하다. Put what you're asking about straight in front with no particle — 피부 관리 어떻게 해요?

examples.en: How do you take care of your skin?
How do you take care of your hair?
How do you take care of your body?

description:
Used to ask whether a product or method really makes a difference.

Rule: 효과 (effect) pairs with 있다 and 없다, not with 하다 — say 효과 있어요? and 효과 없어요, never 효과 해요.

examples.en: Is this serum effective?
Does this diet method work?
Does this medicine work?

description:
Used to say something is well reviewed. Koreans check 후기 before buying almost anything.

Rule: 후기 (review) takes 가 with 좋아요 — 후기가 좋아요. To give the reason for buying, use 후기가 좋아서.

examples.en: The reviews for this cream are amazing!
This restaurant has great reviews — let's go!
I bought it because the reviews were good.

description:
Used to ask about the frequency of a habit or activity.

Rule: 얼마나 (how much) combines with 자주 (often) to ask frequency. Put the verb at the end — 얼마나 자주 운동해요?

examples.en: How often do you exercise?
How often do you go to cafés?
How often do you study Korean?

description:
Used to say something benefits your health — a very common remark about food in Korea.

Rule: 에 marks what the thing is good for, so the pattern is ~에 좋아요. The same shape works elsewhere — 피부에 좋아요 means 'it's good for your skin'.

examples.en: Walking is good for your health!
Kimchi is good for your health.
Sleeping well is good for your health.
examples.ko: 잠 잘 자는 게 건강에 좋아요.

description:
Used to say you've stuck with something over time — exercise, study, a habit.

Rule: 꾸준히 means 'steadily, without breaks'. -고 있어요 marks an action still in progress, so together they mean you started before and are still going.

examples.en: I've been exercising consistently lately!
I've been studying Korean consistently every day.
I've been keeping it up — it's working well!

description:
Used to ask where someone lives. Koreans often narrow it down by area — 서울 어디 살아요?

Rule: 살다 normally takes 에서 for the place, but with 어디 the particle is dropped in speech. Use the present tense 살아요, not the past.

examples.en: Where in Korea do you live?
Where in Seoul do you live?
Where are you living now?

description:
Used to ask whether someone lives by themselves — a normal getting-to-know-you question in Korea.

Rule: 혼자 means 'alone' and goes before the verb. A related word is 자취하다, used for living away from your family, usually as a student.

examples.en: Do you live alone?
Do you live alone? Are you renting on your own?
Isn't it lonely living alone?

description:

description:
Used to list two or more actions or states when either one is possible.

Rule: Attach -거나 to a verb or adjective stem (먹거나, 좋거나). For nouns, use (이)나 instead — 커피나 차 (coffee or tea) after a vowel, 물이나 주스 (water or juice) after a consonant.

examples.en: On weekends I watch movies or read books.
If you're tired or sick, take a rest.
I take the bus or walk.

compare: Use ~(이)나 to link nouns (커피나 차), and -거나 to link verbs or adjectives.

description: Used to add a reason after your main point, as a soft explanation the listener didn't know.

examples.en: I can't go today — I have plans.
He's famous. He's a singer, you see.
I'll be a little late; I just left.

compare: With -어서 or -으니까 the reason comes first. With -거든요 the reason comes after your point.

description: Used when a situation changes by circumstance rather than by your own decision.

examples.en: I ended up living in Korea.
I've come to like spicy food.
We happened to meet.

compare: -어지다 describes a state changing (예뻐지다). -게 되다 describes a situation changing.

description: Used for a guess you make on the spot, or to state your intention politely.

examples.en: It'll probably rain tomorrow.
Wow, that looks delicious!
I'll do it.

compare: -을 거예요 is for a plan already decided. -겠- is for a thought you just had.

description:
Used when something finally happens, usually with regret, or to show firm determination.

Rule: Attach -고 말다 to an action verb only. It normally appears in the past tense (울고 말았어요). The regret meaning is far more common than the determination meaning.

examples.en: I ended up crying.
I ended up losing my wallet.
This time I'll succeed no matter what.

description:
Used to show that the first action was completed before the second one began.

Rule: Both clauses must have the same subject. Never add a tense marker before -고서 — say 먹고서, not 먹었고서.

examples.en: I went out after eating.
I got angry after hearing that.
I felt better after apologizing.

compare: -고 can simply list actions. -고서 makes clear the first action finished first.

description: Used to state the purpose or goal of an action.

examples.en: I came in order to learn Korean.
I walk every day for my health.
I'm working hard to achieve my dream.

compare: -으려고 sounds conversational; -기 위해 sounds more formal or written.

description: Used to say you have decided on something, or to make an agreement with others.

examples.en: I decided to start exercising tomorrow.
Let's agree to meet next week.
I decided to cut back on coffee.

description: Used to give a reason based on something you observed or judged.

examples.en: Since the weather was nice, I took a walk.
It looked good, so I bought it.
I took a taxi since I had no time.

compare: -기에 is more written than -어서, and fits well when your reason is something you saw.

description:
Used to guess about something based on evidence you can see or hear.

Rule: Verbs take -나 보다 (비가 오나 봐요). Adjectives take -은가/-ㄴ가 보다 instead — 좋은가 봐요 (consonant), 바쁜가 봐요 (vowel). Nouns take -인가 보다.

examples.en: There must be a lot of people.
It seems to be raining outside.
That shop must be famous.

compare: -는 것 같다 is your personal impression. -나 보다 is a guess from visible evidence.

description: Used to express a tentative thought or mild doubt about something.

examples.en: I wonder if it's too late.
I think maybe I made a mistake.
I'm not sure if this is right.

description:
Used when something you were doing prevented you from doing something else.

Rule: Both clauses must have the same subject, and the result is always negative. Use it with action verbs only, and never with a command or suggestion.

examples.en: I couldn't call because I was working.
I stayed up all night studying.
I lost track of time watching a drama.
examples.ko: 드라마 보느라고 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요.

compare: 비가 와서 못 갔어요 blames an outside cause. 자느라고 못 갔어요 blames what you yourself were doing.

description:
Used to soften an opinion when you are not fully sure.

Rule: Verbs take -는 것 같기도 (가는 것 같기도 해요). Adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 것 같기도 (좋은 것 같기도, 바쁜 것 같기도). For the past, use -은 것 같기도.

examples.en: It kind of seems right.
It also seems a little difficult.
It might be fine, but I'm not sure.
examples.ko: 괜찮은 것 같기도 한데 잘 모르겠어요.

description: Used to correct a misunderstanding and give the real reason.

examples.en: It's not that I dislike it, it's just a bit much.
It's not that I can't — I just don't.
examples.ko: 못하는 게 아니라 안 하는 거예요.

examples.en: I'm not angry, just tired.

description:
Used to add a second action you can do conveniently while doing the first.

Rule: The first action is the main reason you are there; the second is the extra one. Verbs take -는 김에 for something you are doing now, and -은/-ㄴ 김에 for something already done (온 김에).

examples.en: While I'm out, I'll grab some milk.
examples.ko: 나가는 김에 우유 좀 사 올게요.

examples.en: Since you're here, let's have some tea.
While cleaning, I organized too.

description: Used to say something will happen right after another thing, or to do exactly as told.

examples.en: I'll call as soon as I arrive.
I said it just as I heard it.
I'll go as soon as it's over.

compare: -자마자 means instantly. -는 대로 means as soon as the condition is met, often about plans.

description: Used to replace one thing with another, or to offer something in exchange.

examples.en: I ate bread instead of rice.
Instead of going out, I rested at home.
I'll help you — in return, buy me a coffee.
examples.ko: 제가 도와드리는 대신에 커피 사 주세요.

description:
Used when an unexpected event caused a bad or unintended result.

Rule: The result is always negative and always in the past. Never add a tense marker before it — say 늦는 바람에, not 늦었는 바람에. Do not use it with commands or suggestions.

examples.en: I was late because I overslept.
I couldn't go because it rained.
Things blew up because I posted that photo.

compare: -어서 is neutral. -는 바람에 implies the cause was unexpected and the result unwanted.

description:
Used when you believed something that turned out not to be true.

Rule: Verbs take -는 줄 알았다 (오는 줄 알았어요). Adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 줄 알았다 (좋은 줄 알았어요). Nouns take -인 줄 알았다.

examples.en: I thought it was today.
I thought you were angry.
I thought you were Korean.

description:
Used to describe a general tendency without stating it too strongly.

Rule: Verbs take -는 편이다 (자주 먹는 편이에요). Adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 편이다 — 좋은 편이에요 (consonant), 바쁜 편이에요 (vowel).

examples.en: I'm on the quiet side.
I'm pretty good with spicy food.
This shop is relatively cheap.

description:
Used to report what someone else said or what you heard.

Rule: The ending changes with the word type. Verbs ending in a consonant take -는다고 (먹는다고), verbs ending in a vowel take -ㄴ다고 (간다고), adjectives take -다고 (좋다고), and nouns take -(이)라고 (학생이라고).

examples.en: Jisu said she's coming tomorrow.
I heard this place is good.
He said he's busy these days.

description:
Used to check something you heard about the listener.

Rule: Same form changes as -는다고. Verbs take -는다면서/-ㄴ다면서 (먹는다면서, 간다면서), adjectives take -다면서 (좋다면서), nouns take -(이)라면서. This is casual speech — use -는다면서요? with people you are not close to.

examples.en: I heard you're learning Korean?
I heard you're going next week?
I heard that movie is good?

description:
Used to put a question inside a larger sentence.

Rule: Verbs take -는지 (뭐 먹는지 몰라요). Adjectives take -은/-ㄴ지 (좋은지, 바쁜지). For the past, use -았/었는지.

examples.en: Do you know where it is?
I don't know whether it's right.
I asked why that is.

description:
Used to ask a question in a warm, casual way, often to someone younger or close to you.

Rule: This is 반말. Use it only with close friends, younger people, or family. With anyone else, use -아요/어요? instead.

examples.en: Did you eat?
Where are you going?
Are you okay?

compare: -어? is plain casual. -니? sounds gentler or more caring.

english: as you know; as you can see
description: Used when the listener already knows or can see what you are saying.

examples.en: As you know, today is a day off.
As you can see, it's crowded.
As I mentioned, there's no time.

description:
Used to report something you personally observed and found notable.

Rule: This is 반말 and sounds slightly bookish. In everyday speech -더라 is more natural, and -더군요 is the polite form. You cannot use it about your own feelings or actions.

examples.en: It was bigger than I expected.
Korean food was spicy, I found.
There really were a lot of people.

compare: -더라 is casual and -더군요 is polite, but both report what you saw yourself.

description:
Used to tell a friend about something you experienced yourself.

Rule: This is 반말; the polite form is -더라고요. You must have witnessed it yourself, and you cannot use it to describe your own feelings — say 좋더라 about a place, not about yourself.

examples.en: That cafe was really pretty.
It was easier than I thought.
There were tons of people.

description: Used to suppose something that has not happened yet, and say it won't change the result.

examples.en: Even if it's hard, don't give up.
I'll go even if it rains.
Come even if you're late.

compare: -어도 works for real situations. -더라도 is stronger and used for things that haven't happened.

description:
Used to describe something you did repeatedly in the past or left unfinished.

Rule: Attach -던 to any verb or adjective stem (가던 길, 읽던 책). Use -던 for something repeated or unfinished, and -았/었던 for a single completed event (갔던 곳).

examples.en: It's a cafe I used to go to often.
Please finish what you were eating.
It's the neighborhood I used to live in.

description:
Used to mention something you saw and leave the response to the listener.

Rule: You must have witnessed it yourself, so it cannot describe your own feelings. The polite form is -던데요. For the past, use -았/었던데.

examples.en: Someone was looking for you earlier.
It was cold out — take a jacket.
It was good — give it a try.

english: so that; to the point of
description: Used to state a purpose, or to show the extent something reaches.

examples.en: I left early so I wouldn't be late.
I wrote it big so it's easy to see.
I sang until my throat hurt.

compare: -게 is similar but shorter and more casual; -도록 sounds a little more formal.

description:
Used to ask a question in formal settings such as service, announcements, or interviews.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -습니까 (먹습니까?). After a stem ending in a vowel, use -ㅂ니까 (갑니까?). Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (만들다 → 만듭니까?).

examples.en: Would you like to order?
Where are you from?
Is this time all right for you?

compare: Everyday conversation uses -어요?. Service, announcements and interviews use -습니까?.

description:
Used to make statements in formal settings such as introductions, presentations, or work.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -습니다 (먹습니다). After a stem ending in a vowel, use -ㅂ니다 (갑니다). Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (살다 → 삽니다).

examples.en: Nice to meet you.
I'm from the United States.
Thank you.

compare: Use -어요 with friends. Use -습니다 for introductions, announcements and the workplace.

description:
Used to talk about something that already happened.

Rule: Use -았- after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (가다 → 갔어요, 좋다 → 좋았어요), and -었- after any other vowel (먹다 → 먹었어요). Verbs ending in 하다 become 했- (공부하다 → 공부했어요).

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
I ate.
It was fun.

description:
Used when something is gradually progressing toward a point in the future.

Rule: Choose -아 가다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (살아 가다), -어 가다 elsewhere (되어 가다), and 해 가다 for 하다 verbs. Compare with -어 오다, which looks from the past up to now.

examples.en: It's almost done.
The day is breaking.
I'm slowly getting used to it.

compare: -어 가다 looks forward from now. -어 오다 looks back at what you have done until now.

english: do in advance and leave it
description:
Used when you finish something ahead of time and leave it in that state.

Rule: Choose -아 놓다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (닫아 놓다), -어 놓다 elsewhere (열어 놓다), and 해 놓다 for 하다 verbs. Action verbs only.

examples.en: I'll order it in advance.
I left the window open.
I've got all the ingredients ready.

compare: -어 두다 means almost the same thing; -어 놓다 sounds slightly more conversational.

description:
Used when you do something now and keep the result for later use.

Rule: Choose -아 두다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (사 두다), -어 두다 elsewhere (넣어 두다), and 해 두다 for 하다 verbs. Very close to -어 놓다; -어 두다 stresses keeping it for later.

examples.en: I saved the contact.
I saved us a seat.
I took a photo to keep.

description:
Used to offer to do something for a customer or someone older or senior.

Rule: This is the humble form of -어 주다. Choose -아 드리다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (닦아 드리다), -어 드리다 elsewhere (들어 드리다), and 해 드리다 for 하다 verbs. Never use it about what someone does for you.

examples.en: Let me help you.
Shall I take a photo for you?
I'll show you to your seat.

compare: -어 주다 is for friends and equals. -어 드리다 is the humble form for seniors and customers.

description:
Used when an action is finished off entirely, with relief or regret.

Rule: Choose -아 버리다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (팔아 버리다), -어 버리다 elsewhere (먹어 버리다), and 해 버리다 for 하다 verbs. Action verbs only.

examples.en: I ate it all up.
I burned it.
I forgot.

compare: -고 말다 is similar, but -어 버리다 feels either more relieved or more regretful.

description:
Used to suggest trying something, or to say you have experienced it.

Rule: Choose -아 보다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (가 보다), -어 보다 elsewhere (먹어 보다), and 해 보다 for 하다 verbs. For past experience, use -아/어 봤어요.

examples.en: Try eating it.
May I try it on?
I've been to Korea.

description:
Used for something you have continued doing from the past up to the present.

Rule: Choose -아 오다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (살아 오다), -어 오다 elsewhere (배워 오다), and 해 오다 for 하다 verbs. Compare with -어 가다, which looks toward the future.

examples.en: I've been learning Korean for three years.
I've kept at it steadily.
It's the time we've walked together.

description:
Used to describe the state that remains after an action is finished.

Rule: Choose -아 있다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (앉아 있다), -어 있다 elsewhere (열려 있다). Use it with verbs that have no object — say 앉아 있어요, but 책을 읽고 있어요 for an ongoing action.

examples.en: The flowers are in bloom.
The door is open.
I'm sitting in my seat.

compare: -고 있다 is the action in progress (옷을 입고 있다 = putting it on). -어 있다 is the resulting state (앉아 있다 = seated).

description:
Used when you do something for another person's benefit, or ask them to.

Rule: Choose -아 주다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (도와주다), -어 주다 elsewhere (만들어 주다), and 해 주다 for 하다 verbs. When the other person is older or a customer, use -어 드리다 instead.

examples.en: I'll take a photo for you.
Could you help me a bit?
Please speak slowly.

description:
Used to give a reason, or to connect two actions in order.

Rule: Choose -아서 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (가서, 좋아서), -어서 elsewhere (먹어서), and 해서 for 하다 verbs. Never add a tense marker before it, and never use it before a command or suggestion — use -으니까 for those.

examples.en: I ate because I was hungry.
Sorry I'm late.
I went to a cafe and studied.

compare: -어서 cannot be used before a command or suggestion. Say 늦었으니까 서두르세요, not 늦어서 서두르세요.

description:
Used for a decision you have just made about what you need to do.

Rule: Choose -아야겠다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (가야겠다), -어야겠다 elsewhere (먹어야겠다), and 해야겠다 for 하다 verbs. The subject is almost always 'I'; the polite form is -아/어야겠어요.

examples.en: I should go to bed now.
I'd better pay more attention.
I should start exercising tomorrow.

description:
Used when a state gradually changes into another state.

Rule: Attach it to an adjective stem. Choose -아지다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (좋아지다), -어지다 elsewhere (예뻐지다), and 해지다 for 하다 adjectives (편해지다).

examples.en: Korean has gotten easier.
The weather has gotten warm.
We've gotten a lot closer.

description:
Used to give a reason, especially before a command, suggestion, or invitation.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으니까 (먹으니까). After a vowel, drop the 으 (가니까). Stems ending in ㄹ also drop it (만들다 → 만드니까). Unlike -어서, this one can come before a command.

examples.en: Take an umbrella since it's raining.
Let's hurry since there's no time.
It's good, so give it a try.

compare: Use -어서 for apologies and thanks. Use -으니까 before commands and suggestions.

description:
Used when you move somewhere with a purpose.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으러 (먹으러 가요). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 으 (보러 가요, 놀러 가요). It only works with verbs of movement — 가다 (go), 오다 (come), 다니다 (attend regularly).

examples.en: Let's go eat.
I came to meet a friend.
I went to the bookstore to buy a book.

compare: Only 가다, 오다 and 다니다 can follow -으러. For other verbs use -으려고.

description:
Used to say something is not allowed or not advisable.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으면 (먹으면 안 돼요). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 으 (가면 안 돼요, 만들면 안 돼요).

examples.en: You mustn't take photos here.
You shouldn't overdo it.
You can't throw this away here.

compare: This is the opposite of -어도 되다 (permission), and sounds softer than -지 마세요.

description:
Used when one person does two things at the same time.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으면서 (먹으면서). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 으 (보면서, 만들면서). Both actions must have the same subject.

examples.en: I walk while listening to music.
We talked over coffee.
She said it with a smile.

description:
Used for polite instructions in announcements, notices, and customer service.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으십시오 (앉으십시오). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 으 (가십시오). This is very formal — in everyday conversation use -으세요 instead.

examples.en: Please wait a moment.
Please stand behind the safety line.
Please have a seat.

compare: Everyday speech uses -으세요. Announcements and service settings use -으십시오.

description:
Used to say one action happens after another is finished.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -은 다음에 (먹은 다음에). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 은 (간 다음에, 만든 다음에). Action verbs only.

examples.en: After washing my face, I put on lotion.
I'll go after I eat.
I'll let you know after checking.

description:
Used to say how much time has passed since something happened.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -은 지 (먹은 지). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 은 (온 지, 산 지). Finish with a length of time plus 됐어요 or 지났어요, both meaning 'it has been' — 온 지 2년 됐어요.

examples.en: It's been six months since I came to Korea.
I haven't been learning long.
It's been a long time since we met.

compare: Only 되다, 지나다 and 넘다 follow -은 지. For 'know whether', use -는지 instead.

description:
Used to put two events in order, with the first one finished.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -은 후에 (먹은 후에). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 은 (간 후에). Almost the same as -은 다음에; 후에 sounds slightly more formal.

examples.en: Let's meet after class.
I took a walk after eating.
I'll tell you after I think about it.

description:
Used for a plan you have already decided, or a prediction about the future.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 거예요 (먹을 거예요). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 거예요, 만들 거예요).

examples.en: I'll go tomorrow.
It'll probably rain.
I'm going to keep studying.

compare: -겠어요 is a thought you just had. -을 거예요 is a plan already made.

description:
Used when something happens without fail on each occasion.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 때마다 (먹을 때마다). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 때마다). For nouns, use 마다 directly (날마다).

examples.en: Every time I come here, I feel good.
Every time I hear this song, I think of it.
It looks pretty every time I see it.

description:
Used when there is no other option, or when a result is completely natural.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 수밖에 없다 (먹을 수밖에 없어요). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 수밖에 없어요).

examples.en: I had no choice but to wait.
With this taste, you have to queue.
examples.ko: 이 맛이면 줄 설 수밖에 없어요.

examples.en: Of course you'd be upset.

description:
Used to state your own intention and then ask or suggest something.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 테니 (먹을 테니). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 테니). The first clause is what the speaker will do, so the subject is normally 'I'. -을 테니까 is the more conversational form.

examples.en: I'll do it, so don't worry.
I'll wait, so take your time.
I'll get it ready, so please wait a moment.

description:
Used to guess about someone's situation while showing concern or regret.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 텐데 (먹을 텐데). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 텐데). For a past guess, use -았/었을 텐데 (힘들었을 텐데).

examples.en: It must be hard — are you okay?
Thank you for coming though you must be busy.
It'll be cold — take a jacket.

description:
Used for a casual guess, or to express regret about something you didn't do.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is -을걸요. After a consonant use -을걸 (먹을걸), after a vowel or ㄹ drop the 을 (갈걸). For regret it usually appears as -을걸 그랬어, meaning 'I should have ~'.

examples.en: It's probably closed.
I should have said something then.
I should have booked in advance.

description:
Used to promise the listener that you will do something.

Rule: This is 반말; the polite form is -을게요. After a consonant use -을게 (먹을게), after a vowel or ㄹ drop the 을 (갈게). The subject is always 'I', and it is never used as a question.

examples.en: I'll do it.
I'll call you later.
I'll head out first.

compare: -을 거야 is just your plan. -을게 is a promise made to the listener, so it needs someone to hear it.

description:
Used to suggest doing something together or to offer to do something.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을까요 (먹을까요?). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈까요?, 만들까요?).

examples.en: Shall we go together?
Shall I help you?
What shall we eat?

description:
Used when one thing increases as another increases.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을수록 (먹을수록). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈수록). It often pairs with -으면 in front — 보면 볼수록 means 'the more you look at it'.

examples.en: The more I eat, the better it tastes.
The more you practice, the better you get.
The more I learn, the harder it gets.

compare: Often used together as -으면 -을수록, as in 보면 볼수록.

description:
Used to suggest doing something together in a formal or group setting.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -읍시다 (먹읍시다). After a vowel or ㄹ, use -ㅂ시다 (갑시다). Do not use it toward someone older or senior — use -으시겠어요? (would you like to ~?) instead.

examples.en: Let's toast!
Let's go together.
Let's begin now.

compare: Avoid this with people senior to you; use -으실래요? or -으시죠 instead.

description:
Used when the second action happens immediately after the first.

Rule: Attach -자마자 directly to the verb stem and never add a tense marker before it — say 도착하자마자, not 도착했자마자. The tense is shown in the second clause.

examples.en: I'll go as soon as class ends.
I called as soon as I arrived.
I knew the moment I saw it.

compare: -는 대로 is often about plans. -자마자 stresses that it happened instantly.

description:
Used to remind the listener of something you both already know.

Rule: This is 반말; the polite form is -잖아요. Only use it for information the listener already has — using it for something new sounds rude.

examples.en: I told you yesterday, remember?
We used to come here a lot.
You like it too, don't you?

description: Used to contrast two ideas in one sentence.

examples.en: It's hard but fun.
It was spicy but delicious.
I don't have time, but I want to go.

description:
Used to join two nouns or to say you did something together with someone.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 과 (책과). After a vowel, use 와 (커피와). This pair sounds written or formal; in everyday speech use 하고 or (이)랑.

examples.en: I ate kimchi and rice.
I went with a friend.
Korea and France are different.

compare: ~과/와 is used in writing and formal speech; ~하고 and ~(이)랑 are conversational.

description:
Used when giving or saying something to someone you should show respect to.

Rule: 께 is the honorific form of 에게/한테. Use it for someone older or senior (선생님께), and use 한테 for friends or people your age.

examples.en: I gave it to my teacher.
I wrote a letter to my parents.
I'll tell the boss.

compare: ~께 is the honorific form of ~에게 and ~한테.

description:
Used to mark the subject when that person deserves respect.

Rule: 께서 replaces 이/가 for an honored subject (선생님께서 오셨어요). The verb should also take the honorific -으시- when you use it.

examples.en: The teacher has arrived.
My grandmother made it.
The boss is calling for you.

compare: ~께서 is the honorific form of ~이/가, and the verb usually takes -으시- as well.

description: Used to say something applies to each and every one, without exception.

examples.en: I hike every weekend.
Culture differs from country to country.
Everyone has their own taste.

description: Used to limit something to one thing and nothing else.

examples.en: Just water, please.
Just a little, please.
I was the only one who didn't know.

description: Used to say two things are about the same in degree or amount.

examples.en: It's not as hard as I thought.
I improved as much as I worked at it.
You speak as well as a Korean.

compare: ~보다 points out a difference. ~만큼 says the degree is the same.

description:
Used to say there is nothing more than this; always followed by a negative.

Rule: The verb must be negative — say 물밖에 없어요, never 물밖에 있어요. It replaces 이/가 and 을/를, so do not stack particles.

examples.en: I only have a thousand won.
Only one person came.
This is all I can do.

compare: ~만 takes a positive verb (물만 주세요). ~밖에 must be followed by a negative.

description: Used to mark the starting point and the end point of time or place.

examples.en: I work from 9 to 6.
I'm going from Seoul to Busan.
I watched it from start to finish.

description: Used to say that is the whole of it and there is nothing else.

examples.en: You're the only one I can trust.
It's only once.
I just smiled, that's all.

description:
Used to mark the person who receives something or is spoken to.

Rule: 한테 is for everyday speech, 에게 is for writing and formal speech, and 께 is the honorific form. For animals use 한테/에게; for places or organizations use 에 instead.

examples.en: I gave a gift to my friend.
Ask me.
I told my younger sibling.

compare: ~에게 is written, ~한테 is spoken. Both are only for people and animals; use ~에 for places.

description: Used to emphasize the starting point of a movement or process.

examples.en: I walked starting from here.
I came all the way from Seoul.
Let's start over from the very beginning.

description:
Used to mark a direction, a means of doing something, or a material.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 으로 (손으로). After a vowel or ㄹ, use 로 (버스로, 지하철로).

examples.en: I go by subway.
Go to the right.
This is made with beans.

description:
Used to casually ask what the other person wants to do.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을래요 (먹을래요?). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈래요?). It is friendly rather than formal, so avoid it with someone senior.

examples.en: Would you like to go together?
What would you like to drink?
Want to sing a song?

compare: -을까요? proposes doing it together. -을래요? asks what the listener wants.

description:
Used when something is not enough but is still better than nothing.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이나마 (조금이나마). After a vowel, drop the 이 (잠시나마).

examples.en: I rested, if only briefly.
I want to help, even if only a little.
Please take this, small as it is.

description:
Used to raise a topic or to define what something really is.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이란 (사랑이란). After a vowel, drop the 이 (친구란). It sounds thoughtful or literary, so it fits reflections more than casual chat.

examples.en: What is happiness, anyway?
That's what friends are for.
Korean is really interesting.

description:
Used to say what something or someone is; the most basic way to make a statement.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이에요 (학생 → 학생이에요). After a noun ending in a vowel, use 예요 (커피 → 커피예요).

examples.en: I'm a student.
This is yuja tea.
My name is Emma.

compare: Use 이에요 after a final consonant (학생이에요) and 예요 after a vowel (차예요).

description: Used to compare something to another thing it resembles.

examples.en: You speak like a Korean.
It's pretty like a petal.
Let's meet like yesterday.

compare: ~같이 means almost the same; ~처럼 sounds slightly more written.

description:
Used to say that not only the bigger thing but even the smaller thing was impossible.

Rule: With nouns it appears as 은커녕 after a consonant (밥은커녕) and 는커녕 after a vowel (커피는커녕). With verbs, use -기는커녕 (쉬기는커녕). The second clause is always negative.

examples.en: Far from traveling, I don't even have time to rest.
Instead of praise, I got scolded.
I couldn't even drink water, let alone eat.

description:
Used in everyday speech to join nouns or to say you did something with someone.

Rule: 하고 attaches the same way to any noun, with no consonant rule. It is the most conversational option; (이)랑 is even more casual and 과/와 is formal.

examples.en: Tteokbokki and sundae, please.
I went with a friend.
Come with me.

description: Used to mark the person something was received or heard from.

examples.en: I heard it from a friend.
I got it from my older sister.
Who did you learn it from?

compare: ~에게서 is written, ~한테서 is spoken. Use these when the person is the source.

description: Used to ask how much time something will take, such as travel, delivery, or cooking.

examples.en: How long does it take from here?
How long does it take to cook?
How long does it take by subway?

description: Used to ask what you should not miss when visiting a place.

examples.en: What's a must-see in Jeju?
examples.ko: 제주도에서 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요?

examples.en: What's a must-see in Seoul?
examples.ko: 서울에서 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요?

examples.en: What's a must-see in this neighborhood?
examples.ko: 이 동네에서 꼭 봐야 할 게 뭐예요?
